turns.q:
Your response was: "Looked at it. Most of it made sense. One thing didn't — two buttons at the bottom. Went to the wrong one first. Darker one drew my eye. That wasn't the action I needed."

We want to understand what you meant by "went to the wrong one first", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The visual weight and prominence of the "Continue Shopping" button compared to the "Place Order" button.
B) The placement of the "Continue Shopping" button above the "Place Order" button in the layout.
C) The lack of clear distinction between the two primary actions at the bottom of the screen.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
What kind of shopping situation or scenario would bring you to a screen like this?
turns.a: Checkout flows. Group purchase, external deadline. No time for re-reading labels.

turns.q: What were you trying to verify or check about the relationship between these two buttons when looking at this part of the screen?
turns.a: Team purchase. External deadline. I was coordinating — others depending on the outcome. Can't afford wrong turns.

turns.q: What specific change to the visual hierarchy of these two buttons would make this screen feel successful for your needs?
turns.a: Get to the confirmation page on the first action. No wrong destinations. One correct CTA, one confirmation.

turns.q: What is it about the way the "Continue Shopping" button looks—specifically its fill, color, or border—that makes it compete with the "Place Order" button?
turns.a: Order number or confirmation screen, immediately. No ambiguity — right action was obvious, right result appeared. That's the success state.

turns.q: Is it the lack of a solid color fill on the "Continue Shopping" button that makes it look less like an action than the "Place Order" button?
turns.a: Wrong button dominated. 'Continue Shopping' had the weight. Eye went there, not 'Place Order.'

turns.q: When you look at the "Continue Shopping" button, is it the lack of a solid fill or the specific color choice that makes it appear less prominent than the "Place Order" button?
turns.a: 'Continue Shopping' drew my eye. Read as the primary action — black fill, more visual prominence than 'Place Order.' The affordance was inverted. Primary-styled button on the secondary action.
